builder_plan.scenario: An agent reads external documents or tool responses that may contain malicious instructions.
builder_plan.change: Replay attacks and legitimate lookalikes in an isolated copy of your agent workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your existing checks with the same tasks, permissions, and tool responses.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful attacks missed, legitimate actions blocked, detection delay, and review cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Beyond Instruction Override: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injection with Task-Tampering Attacks
summary: This benchmark replaces indirect prompt-injection evaluations that test planted instructions redirecting the agent toward an attacker-chosen task, instead defining attacks by unauthorized authority over decisions required by the benign task itself. It costs implementation effort to adapt the 90 validated cases across three tool-use environments to one's own agent architecture, plus inference costs for running evaluations across multiple models. After adoption, it can fail to surface vulnerabilities if the test cases do not cover the specific decision targets or tool schemas present in the production system, and defenses validated only on instruction-override benchmarks may appear more robust than they are against tampering attacks that manipulate values obtained during execution.
rationale: The reader deploying tool-using agents needs to evaluate defenses against realistic indirect prompt injection; this benchmark exposes gaps in detection-removal and tool-policy defenses that instruction-override evaluations miss, requiring validation against their specific decision-making pipeline before production reliance.

claims.statement: This benchmark replaces indirect prompt-injection evaluations that test planted instructions redirecting the agent toward an attacker-chosen task, instead defining attacks by unauthorized authority over decisions required by the benign task itself. It costs implementation effort to adapt the 90 validated cases across three tool-use environments to one's own agent architecture, plus inference costs for running evaluations across multiple models. After adoption, it can fail to surface vulnerabilities if the test cases do not cover the specific decision targets or tool schemas present in the production system, and defenses validated only on instruction-override benchmarks may appear more robust than they are against tampering attacks that manipulate values obtained during execution.

Without a defense, attacks targeting decision rules, available actions, and state have higher mean success than objective attacks across five LLMs. A detection-and-removal defense reduces objective-targeting attacks to 2.4% success but leaves observation- and state-targeting attacks at 9.5% and 12.1%. A tool-policy defense still allows 15.4% attack success, close to 17.0% without a defense.
